chapters.title: Chapter 2: Covariance, Correlation, and the Mathematics of Diversification

lessons.title: Extending to N Assets: Building the Covariance Matrix

children.text: The last lesson's formula had three terms because it covered exactly two assets. Real portfolios hold far more than two. This lesson extends the same idea to any number of assets, and introduces the notation quant desks actually use once the term count gets too large to write out by hand.

body.text: For N assets, portfolio variance sums a term for every possible PAIR of assets, including each asset paired with itself. N assets create N squared terms in total. This is exactly why practitioners switch from writing sums longhand to matrix algebra.

children.text: From a Pair to N Assets: the General Formula

body.caption: Portfolio variance for N assets: sum over every ordered pair (i, j), including i = j. When i = j, Cov_ii is just Var_i.

children.text: Set N to 2 and this formula reproduces Lesson 2 exactly. The double sum runs over four (i, j) pairs: (1,1), (1,2), (2,1), and (2,2). The (1,1) and (2,2) terms are w1 squared Var1 and w2 squared Var2. The (1,2) and (2,1) terms are both equal to w1 w2 Cov12, since covariance does not care about order, and adding them together produces the familiar 2 w1 w2 Cov12 cross term. Nothing new happened between Lesson 2 and here. The same idea just now runs for any N, not only 2.
Matrix Notation: the Same Thing, Written Compactly

Writing out a double sum for 50 stocks means 2,500 terms on the page. Nobody does that by hand. Instead, collect the weights into a column vector w, and the covariance matrix from Lesson 1 into a grid called Sigma. The entire double sum above collapses into one expression.

body.caption: The same formula, in matrix notation. w is the column vector of weights, Sigma is the covariance matrix, and w^T is that vector laid on its side.

children.text: Read as a mechanical recipe, not abstract algebra: multiply the covariance matrix by the weight vector, which blends each asset's row of covariances by how much of it you hold, then multiply that result by the weights again, laid sideways, to collapse everything down to one number. Every quant tool from Excel's SUMPRODUCT on a covariance matrix to Python's numpy performs exactly this calculation, they simply do it without you writing out the (i, j) pairs yourself.
Worked Example: a Four-Stock Covariance Matrix

Add HDFC Bank and Hindustan Unilever to TCS and Maruti Suzuki. Instead of computing covariances from raw return series as earlier lessons did, this is how it is usually done in practice: estimate each stock's annualized volatility, estimate the pairwise correlations, then multiply them together to build the covariance matrix.

Multiplying each correlation by the two stocks' volatilities, Cov_ij = rho_ij x sigma_i x sigma_j, turns the correlation matrix into a covariance matrix. Notice the FMCG stock, HUL, carries the lowest correlation against every other name here, which is exactly what Chapter 1 predicted for a sector with a genuinely different demand driver.

The diagonal, 484, 784, 625, and 324, is just each stock's own variance, its volatility squared. Now equal-weight the four stocks at 25% each and run w^T Sigma w. The four diagonal terms, each weight squared times its own variance, sum to 138.56. The six off-diagonal pairs, each counted twice as the formula requires, sum to 96.56. Total portfolio variance is 235.13, and the square root of that is a portfolio standard deviation of 15.33%.

stats.label: Naive average of the four vols
Reduction from naive
stats.context: The diversification benefit across four moderately correlated stocks

body.code:
import numpy as np

vols = np.array([22, 28, 25, 18])  # TCS, Maruti, HDFC Bank, HUL
corr = np.array([
    [1.00, 0.30, 0.25, 0.10],
    [0.30, 1.00, 0.35, 0.15],
    [0.25, 0.35, 1.00, 0.20],
    [0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 1.00],
])

# Covariance matrix: Cov_ij = corr_ij * vol_i * vol_j
cov_matrix = corr * np.outer(vols, vols)

weights = np.array([0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25])
portfolio_variance = weights @ cov_matrix @ weights
portfolio_vol = np.sqrt(portfolio_variance)

print(f"Portfolio variance: {portfolio_variance:.2f}")
print(f"Portfolio volatility: {portfolio_vol:.2f}%")
# Portfolio variance: 235.13
# Portfolio volatility: 15.33%
body.caption: weights @ cov_matrix @ weights is exactly w^T Sigma w. np.outer(vols, vols) builds the sigma_i x sigma_j grid before multiplying elementwise by the correlation matrix.

children.text: The Hidden Cost: How Many Numbers You Actually Need

A covariance matrix is symmetric, Cov_ij always equals Cov_ji, so you do not need to estimate every one of the N squared cells separately. But the number of genuinely unique values, N variances plus N times (N minus 1) divided by 2 distinct covariances, still grows fast.

body.caption: Unique parameters needed to fully specify a covariance matrix

body.text: A 50-stock portfolio needs 1,275 separate numbers estimated correctly, mostly correlations, each one built from a limited history of noisy data. Get even a handful of those pairwise correlations wrong, and w^T Sigma w happily returns a confident, precise-looking, and wrong answer. Chapter 5 is dedicated entirely to this estimation problem, one of the main reasons textbook Markowitz optimization is harder to run well in practice than the formula alone suggests.

body.title: Reading the covariance matrix
body.question: In a covariance matrix for five stocks, what sits on the diagonal, and how many unique off-diagonal covariance values are there?
options: Each stock's expected return sits on the diagonal, and there are 5 unique covariances
Each stock's own variance sits on the diagonal, and there are 10 unique covariances
Zeros sit on the diagonal, and there are 25 unique covariances
Each stock's own variance sits on the diagonal, and there are 25 unique covariances
body.explanation: The diagonal holds each asset's own variance, since Cov_ii is just Var_i. Off the diagonal, there are 5 x 4 = 20 cells, but the matrix is symmetric, so only 20 / 2 = 10 of them are genuinely unique, matching N(N-1)/2 with N = 5.

cards.definition: sigma_p^2 = sum over i and j of w_i w_j Cov_ij, a double sum over every pair of assets, including each asset with itself.
The matrix form of the same formula. w is the weight vector, Sigma is the covariance matrix. Standard notation across quant tools and textbooks.
The property that Cov_ij always equals Cov_ji, meaning a covariance matrix is a mirror image of itself across its diagonal.
The number of unique variance and covariance values needed to fully specify a covariance matrix for N assets, combining N variances and N(N-1)/2 distinct covariances.

points: Portfolio variance for N assets is a double sum over every pair (i, j), which for N = 2 collapses exactly to Lesson 2's three-term formula.
The matrix form, sigma_p^2 = w^T Sigma w, is the same calculation written compactly, and is what every real portfolio tool actually computes.
In practice, covariance matrices are usually built from separately estimated volatilities and a correlation matrix, then multiplied together, rather than computed directly from raw return series.
Applied to four Nifty 50 stocks across sectors, this formula gave a portfolio volatility of 15.33%, well below the naive 23.25% average of the four individual volatilities.
A covariance matrix is symmetric, but the number of genuinely unique values still grows quickly: 1,275 for 50 assets, and over a lakh for 500.
More assets means more covariances to estimate correctly, each one only as reliable as the data behind it. This is the seed of Chapter 5's estimation-error problem.
